overview: Zhangzhung was a western plateau polity later absorbed by Tibet. The atlas assigns it 400 to 1 BCE, many centuries before the seventh-century political events described in historical scholarship. Its broad outline is not an established ancient frontier. The early settlements below reveal regional life, but archaeology alone does not identify their inhabitants as subjects of a named Zhangzhung king.

periods.title: The atlas’s early archaeological window
periods.summary: Regional settlement evidence belongs here; later political and religious accounts must be dated separately.

items.text: Bon traditions preserve rich accounts of Zhangzhung’s sacred places and teachers. Bellezza’s field inventory stresses that most relevant Bon literary sources were written after the eleventh century CE. They matter as religious memory and can suggest places to investigate, but cannot simply supply a royal calendar for 400 BCE.

At Jiweng, a rectangular stone enclosure of about 960 square metres dates to approximately 391 to 208 BCE. Excavators found very few objects, including an almost complete red pottery vessel. They interpret the simple site as a possible seasonal camp, rather than a crowded permanent town.

Dingdong preserves eleven stone structures; three partly underground domestic spaces were excavated. Researchers interpret it as a year-round farming and herding village. Its occupation ranges from about 348 BCE to 541 CE, so its houses belong to a long sequence extending well beyond this map window.

sections.title: Food and the work behind it

items.text: Charred barley from hearths at Jiweng and Dingdong brings us close to everyday cooking. Grains and other cereal parts support local cultivation in high western valleys by about 400 BCE. A burnt seed may survive long after the meal, the cook and the cooking pot have gone.

Both hulled and naked barley occur among the finds. “Naked” barley sheds its outer husk more easily; hulled barley takes extra processing before eating. Choosing grain could affect household chores as well as harvests. The exact importance of the less common hulled type remains uncertain.

At Piyang, modern village expansion exposed charcoal, pottery and animal bones. Researchers sampled the deposits and dated the early activity to about 396 to 212 BCE. An ordinary construction project unexpectedly opened a window onto a much older settlement.

A 2024 study examined chemical signatures in barley from Jiweng, Piyang and Dingdong. The grains suggest well-watered growing conditions. Researchers propose deliberate watering or choosing naturally damp plots. This is evidence about crop management, not an excavated canal system stretching across the plateau.

The same study found nutrient signatures consistent with improving fields, probably using animal manure. Herding and farming could help one another: animals supplied more than meat and wool. Their dung could help grow the next crop, although natural soil conditions also affect the measurements.

sections.title: Objects with a life before burial

items.text: Chuvthag’s earlier Zone II cemetery contains a painted wooden tray with animal and bird designs. Small holes and surviving thread show that its broken feet had been repaired before burial. Someone had kept a useful, decorated possession going instead of replacing it.

Woodworkers also carved basins from single blocks, mostly birch, adding handles on both sides. Many still contained food remains when excavated at Chuvthag. These are burial offerings, but they preserve the shapes and working materials of containers familiar in daily life.

The cemeteries span centuries around the beginning of the Common Era; Zone II is earlier than Zone I. Ordered grave arrangements led excavators to suggest possible clan burial grounds. That is an interpretation of shared planning, not proof that every person buried together belonged to one biological family.

At Gekhö Kharlung, a small piece of wood from a partly underground building yielded a date of roughly 200 BCE to 100 CE. It provides an early clue for the site’s use, although a loose wood fragment cannot date every surviving wall or prove a king lived there.

Upper Tibetan builders made some roofs entirely from stone. Projecting supports carried bridging stones, which held roof slabs; several small rooms could form a larger complex. Bellezza’s surveyed examples span an incompletely dated tradition. The technique shows ingenious construction, but is not all securely dated before 1 BCE.

Much later, seventh-century accounts place Zhangzhung within Tibetan expansion. A royal-marriage story features the Tibetan princess Sad-mar-kar and a Zhangzhung ruler. Scholars debate details of the narrative; it offers evidence of how political relationships were remembered, rather than a reliable explanation of an entire war through one unhappy marriage.

Zhangzhung survived in Bon religious learning long after its independent political history. A bilingual dictionary published in Delhi in 1965 collected expressions from sacred texts, helping linguists compare Zhangzhung and Tibetan. These later written traditions preserve valuable language material while presenting difficult questions about earlier forms and transmission.

A short example is ཏིང་, ting, meaning “water.” This is a modern Tibetan-script rendering of the Zhangzhung word listed in Matisoff’s 2001 scholarly study. It represents later preserved vocabulary, not a surviving inscription from 400 to 1 BCE. No contemporary written sample from that atlas interval is established here.

ending.text: The atlas cutoff at 1 BCE is not Zhangzhung’s fall. Scholarship generally places its annexation by the expanding Tibetan kingdom around 644 or 645 CE. Political independence ended, while inhabitants became part of a changing Tibetan world; the Zhangzhung language and sacred past remained subjects of Bon transmission and later scholarship.
